# Results — Study 374 (Vol-of-Vol 🌀)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). **VVIX** — the CBOE
"volatility of the VIX" (the VIX construction applied to VIX *options*) — tested as an
equity-risk timer **against the VIX itself**. We fetch `^VVIX`, `^VIX` and `SPY`
(yfinance, auto-adjusted), build a point-in-time "high vol-of-vol" state (VVIX above its
trailing 252-day 80th percentile), and measure forward SPY returns/drawdowns vs the base
rate — then run the decisive **incremental** test: a Newey-West (HAC) regression of forward
returns on standardized VIX **and** VVIX. Offline core + synthetic control are
deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily closes — `^VVIX`, `^VIX`, `SPY` (auto-adjusted; public, no key) |
| Window | 2007-01-03 → 2026-06-18 (**4,887** trading days; **19.5** years) |
| As-of | 2026-06-18 (last complete bar ≤ 2026-06-22; partial bars dropped) |
| Signal | "high vol-of-vol" = VVIX > trailing **252-day 80th percentile** (causal, point-in-time) |
| Horizons | forward **1-month (21d)** and **3-month (63d)** SPY return / drawdown |
| Entry / costs | 1-day execution lag; timing rule charged **2 bps** one-way per position change |

> **Why VVIX starts in 2007.** CBOE's VVIX history begins in 2007, so the sample spans the
> GFC, the 2011/2015/2018 vol shocks and the 2020 COVID crash — vol-of-vol's natural
> habitat. `SPY` is auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested); the VIX/VVIX are index levels
> (no total-return distinction). All three series are price/level inputs, not strategies.

## The raw signal — forward SPY after a high-VVIX day vs the base rate

1-day entry lag; the unconditional column is *all* overlapping forward windows on the same
tape (the honest base rate). The Welch *t* compares the conditional mean to the
unconditional mean; the placebo *p* is the share of 20,000 block-resampled random date sets
whose mean forward return is **as low as** the high-VVIX set (we test for *under*-performance).

| horizon | n high-VVIX | cond. mean | cond. win | base mean | base win | Welch *t* | placebo *p* | cond. drawdown | base drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-month | 1,059 | **+1.44%** | 69% | +0.99% | 67% | **+2.35** | 0.93 | **−5.37%** | −4.13% |
| 3-month | 1,046 | **+3.89%** | 73% | +2.92% | 73% | **+3.51** | 0.97 | **−8.75%** | −7.66% |

Read it carefully — the surprise is the **sign**. The believers expect high vol-of-vol to
precede *weak* returns. Instead forward returns after high VVIX are **higher**, not lower
(+1.44% vs +0.99% at 1m, Welch *t* = +2.35), because VVIX spikes cluster at **crash
bottoms that then rebound** (2008-Q4, 2020-Q1, 2011, 2018). The placebo *p* ≈ 0.93/0.97
confirms it: almost no random draw is *as low* as the high-VVIX set, because the high-VVIX
set isn't low at all. What *does* survive is the **drawdown** read: high VVIX precedes
deeper peak-to-trough pain (−5.37% vs −4.13%) — it flags turbulence, not direction.

## The decisive test — does VVIX beat the VIX *incrementally*?

The whole claim is "**better than the VIX itself**." VIX and VVIX co-move, so a raw VVIX
signal can look predictive just because high VVIX co-occurs with high VIX. The honest test
is a bivariate regression with **Newey-West (HAC)** standard errors at the overlap lag:

| horizon | model | VIX coef (HAC *t*) | VVIX coef (HAC *t*) |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| 1-month | VIX only | +0.45% (**1.14**) | — |
| 1-month | VVIX only | — | +0.59% (**2.28**) |
| 1-month | **VIX + VVIX** | +0.25% (0.57) | **+0.49% (1.57)** |
| 3-month | VIX only | +0.95% (0.82) | — |
| 3-month | VVIX only | — | +1.27% (1.74) |
| 3-month | **VIX + VVIX** | +0.51% (0.39) | **+1.06% (1.12)** |

There is the verdict. On its own, the 1-month VVIX coefficient clears the bar (HAC *t* =
**2.28**). But **once VIX is in the model, VVIX's *t* collapses to 1.57** (and 1.12 at 3
months) — below the desk's *t* ≥ 2. The corr(VIX, VVIX) ≈ **0.41** is enough that most of
the raw VVIX "signal" is VIX leaking through. VVIX does **not** carry robust *incremental*
information about forward equity returns beyond the VIX. (Note both fail in the believers'
direction anyway — the coefficient is *positive*.)

## Robustness — the raw Welch *t* is threshold-fragile

| VVIX state quantile | n high-VVIX | cond. 1m mean | base | Welch *t* | cond. drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.70 | 1,567 | +1.08% | +0.99% | **0.56** | −5.17% |
| **0.80** | 1,059 | +1.44% | +0.99% | **2.35** | −5.37% |
| 0.90 | 556 | +1.60% | +0.99% | **2.25** | −6.06% |

Drop the threshold to the 70th percentile and the raw Welch *t* falls to **0.56**. The
"significant" raw number lives in a narrow band of the most extreme tail — exactly the
selection fragility a single robust incremental test is designed to expose.

## Tradability — a long/flat timer barely matches, and loses net

A "go to cash when vol-of-vol is high, else hold SPY" rule (1-day lag, 2 bps one-way):

| book | ann. return | ann. vol | Sharpe | trades | time flat |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **strategy** (net @ 2 bps) | +8.9% | 13.7% | **0.65** | 414 | 22% |
| buy & hold SPY | +12.4% | 19.6% | **0.63** | — | — |

The timer's Sharpe (0.65 net) is statistically a tie with buy-and-hold (0.63) — it trades
~3.5pp of annual return for ~6pp of vol, which any cash blend would also buy. With no
*incremental* signal over VIX and a Sharpe race that's a wash, there is no deployable edge
here.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine isolates incremental vol-of-vol

A deterministic tape where VVIX = a VIX component **plus an independent vol-of-vol
component**, and the planted edge lives **only** in the part of VVIX that VIX cannot see:

| planted incremental edge | corr(VIX,VVIX) | VVIX-only HAC *t* | VVIX-over-VIX HAC *t* | VVIX coef |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no edge) | 0.37 | −0.83 | **−1.52** | −0.50% |
| **+0.04** (large) | 0.37 | −14.16 | **−15.84** | −13.01% |
| **+0.10** (huge) | 0.37 | −17.76 | **−19.85** | −22.82% |

With **no** planted edge the incremental VVIX *t* stays inside ±2 (no false positive); a
planted edge — and only an edge in the VIX-orthogonal part of VVIX — drives the
*incremental* *t* to −16/−20 with the correct (negative, drawdown-y) sign. The control
proves two things: the HAC machinery is unbiased, **and** it specifically isolates
*incremental* vol-of-vol signal, not VIX bleeding through. On the real tape that
incremental *t* is ~1.1–1.6 — exactly what *no incremental edge* looks like.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** Raw high-VVIX days do precede slightly *higher* mean returns (Welch
  *t* = 2.35 at 1m) and deeper drawdowns — a real but **direction-confused** pattern (it
  flags turbulence, not down-moves). The claim under test, "**times risk better than the
  VIX**," fails the decisive test: once VIX is controlled, VVIX's HAC *t* is **1.57 / 1.12**
  — below 2 — and the raw *t* is threshold-fragile (0.56 at the 70th pct). Literature + a
  positive-but-non-robust, non-incremental point estimate ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The long/flat timer's net Sharpe (0.65) ties buy-and-hold (0.63)
  — it buys vol reduction any cash blend would, at the cost of return. With no incremental
  signal over the VIX you already track for free, there is no NAV-scale edge in the
  vol-of-vol.
- **Better than the VIX? — BUSTED.** The selling point is *incremental* timing power. The
  HAC regression says VVIX adds nothing robust once VIX is in the model: the raw VVIX *t* of
  2.28 is mostly the 0.41-correlated VIX leaking through. Vol-of-vol is a redundant cousin of
  vol, not a sharper risk clock.
